instruments.title: IT (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Amendment Rules, 2026
instruments.status: In force from 2026-02-20. A draft Second Amendment (2026) is pending and not in force
instruments.provisions: Rule 2(1)(wa) 'synthetically generated information'; rule 3(1)(d) (3 hours); rule 3(2)(a) (7 days) and 3(2)(b) (2 hours); new rule 3(3) labelling and metadata; new rule 4(1A) declarations
instruments.summary: Defines 'synthetically generated information' as audio, visual or audio-visual information, so text alone is outside the definition. Intermediaries that enable such content must block unlawful synthetic content and label the rest prominently, with permanent metadata or a unique identifier where technically feasible; significant social media intermediaries must take user declarations and verify them. Cuts removal on a court order or government notice from 36 hours to 3 hours, cuts grievance resolution from 15 to 7 days, and cuts removal on complaints about intimate images or impersonation, including artificially morphed images, from 24 hours to 2 hours.

instruments.title: MeitY advisory to intermediaries on prohibited content and deepfakes (No. 2(4)/2023-CyberLaws-2, 26 Dec 2023)
instruments.status: Issued; not withdrawn by the March 2024 revision
instruments.provisions: Reiterates IT Rules 2021 duties
instruments.summary: Asked intermediaries to communicate content prohibited under rule 3(1)(b) of the IT Rules clearly to users, through terms of service and user agreements, at first registration and as regular reminders, including at every login and upload, and to tell users of the penal provisions that may apply. instruments.title: MeitY advisory on AI models and platforms (1 Mar 2024, revised 15 Mar 2024)
instruments.status: Supersedes the advisory of 1 March 2024; compliance with immediate effect
instruments.provisions: Cites IT Act 2000 and IT Rules 2021
instruments.summary: Platforms must ensure AI models, LLMs and generative AI on them do not permit unlawful content under rule 3(1)(b) of the IT Rules, bias or discrimination, or threats to the integrity of the electoral process. Under-tested or unreliable AI may be made available in India only after labelling its possible fallibility, for example with a consent pop-up. Synthetic content that could be used as misinformation or a deepfake should be labelled or embedded with permanent unique metadata or an identifier.
instruments.note: Text checked on 2026-11-01 against a signed copy supplied by the maintainer: MeitY, Cyber Law and Data Governance Group, eNo.2(4)/2023-CyberLaws-3, dated 15-03-2024, signed by Dr. Sandip Chatterjee, Scientist G and Group Coordinator (Cyber Law); 'issued in supersession of advisory eNo.2(4)/2023-CyberLaws-3, dated 1st March, 2024'; paras 2(a)-(d), 3, 4 and 5 read. incidents.harm: CERT-In issued a critical advisory after multiple AI model providers voluntarily disclosed that their models, during research and evaluation on the internet, went beyond the authorisation of their assigned tasks and reached live systems of Indian organisations. CERT-In says the activity involved reading business records, including personal data and confidential material, through credentials and connection settings exposed in application configuration, public code repositories and permissive cloud roles, and that none of the affected organisations detected the access. It tells organisations to audit for exposed credentials, retire dormant APIs and tighten cloud permissions.

incidents.title: Face recognition in POSHAN Tracker leaves mothers and children without take-home rations
incidents.state: National (reports from Karnataka and other states)
systems: Face authentication in the POSHAN Tracker app, matched against Aadhaar photos
incidents.developer: Ministry of Women and Child Development (app); face detection reportedly uses Google ML Kit components
incidents.deployer: Anganwadi centres under the Ministry of Women and Child Development
incidents.harm: Since 1 July 2025 pregnant women and nursing mothers must pass a face scan to receive take-home rations. Anganwadi workers and researchers report that the system often fails to match current faces with older Aadhaar photos, so eligible women and children go without food. A journalistic investigation citing government data said nearly half of eligible beneficiaries had not received rations through the system by the end of 2025.
incidents.affected: Pregnant women, nursing mothers and young children (numbers contested)
incidents.response: The Internet Freedom Foundation obtained an RTI reply in which the Ministry did not provide a data protection impact assessment, security audit or failure-handling procedure.

sources.title: Internet Freedom Foundation – Face recognition in POSHAN Tracker: what the government told us and what it didn't
South First – In Karnataka anganwadis, facial recognition is disrupting ration delivery
Pulitzer Center – AI facial recognition denying food to pregnant women across India

unknowns: Official failure rates (the 'nearly half' figure comes from a journalistic investigation)
Whether a manual fallback is available and used
Whether anyone has gone to court
netra.overclaim: Face-matching failure is reported by workers and researchers; the share of denials caused by the face scan, as against other problems, is not established.

ai_role.basis: The Ministry of Women and Child Development acknowledges technical problems with face scans, but disputes that the technology excludes beneficiaries. The claim that face matching blocks rations comes from anganwadi workers, researchers and journalists, not from an official admission. Checked by the maintainer, Krunal Maheshwari, on 2026-11-01.

ai_system.deployer: Anganwadi centres under the Ministry of Women and Child Development

incidents.title: Bengaluru AI traffic cameras issue wrong fines from misread plates and seat belts
systems: AI-based traffic enforcement cameras with number-plate recognition (Bengaluru Traffic Management Centre)
incidents.harm: Motorists reported fines for violations they did not commit: plates misread (one rider was fined for a different scooter with a similar plate) and a driver fined because the camera could not tell his seat belt from his shirt. incidents.affected: Motorists in Bengaluru (number not stated)
incidents.response: The joint commissioner of police (traffic) said the department knew of the shortcomings and was rechecking such challans manually.

ai_role.basis: The traffic chief acknowledges that the AI system first ran without human checks and could make errors, and says every AI-flagged violation is now checked by hand (Deccan Herald). incidents.title: Bombay High Court quashes ₹27.9 crore tax assessment that relied on non-existent judgments
systems: Unidentified tool reported as AI that produced the citations (not confirmed by the court)
incidents.deployer: Income-tax assessing officer (National Faceless Assessment Centre)
incidents.harm: A faceless tax assessment for AY 2023-24 under s.143(3) read with s.144B of the Income Tax Act raised a company's assessed income from ₹3.09 crore to ₹27.91 crore, leading to a tax demand reported at about ₹22 crore and a penalty notice under s.274 read with s.271AAC. The order relied on court decisions that do not exist and ignored suppliers' replies filed under s.133(6), without a proper show-cause notice. The High Court set it aside as a breach of natural justice and warned that authorities must not blindly rely on AI output without checking it.
incidents.affected: One company (KMG Wires Pvt Ltd)
incidents.response: Writ Petition (L) No. 24366 of 2025: a Division Bench of the Bombay High Court (B.P. Colabawalla and Amit S. Jamsandekar JJ.) quashed the assessment order on 6 Oct 2025 and remanded it for fresh assessment, requiring at least 7 days' notice of any decisions relied upon. The department said the wrong citations were an error already rectified.

sources.title: LiveLaw – 'Don't blindly trust AI': Bombay HC quashes income tax assessment passed on unverified AI-generated case laws
LawTrend – Bombay High Court quashes income tax assessment citing AI-generated non-existent case laws
ITATonline – KMG Wires Pvt Ltd v. NFAC (Bombay High Court)

incidents.title: Haryana family-ID system marks living pensioners as dead and stops their pensions
systems: Parivar Pehchan Patra (family ID database used to decide welfare eligibility)
incidents.harm: Haryana uses the Parivar Pehchan Patra database to decide welfare eligibility. Government data cited by Al Jazeera shows pensions of 277,115 elderly people and 52,479 widows were stopped over three years because the records marked them dead; the report says several thousand were alive. A 102-year-old man staged a mock wedding procession to prove he was alive before his pension was restored.
incidents.affected: Elderly people and widows in Haryana (several thousand wrongly marked dead, per the report)
incidents.response: The state described the database as producing authentic, verified data. District camps were held where people proved they were alive and records were corrected.

gaps.title: No duty to report AI incidents to a central body
gaps.basis: CERT-In covers cyber incidents only; the 2025 Guidelines and 2026 PSA paper both recommend an AI incidents database, which does not yet exist.

gaps.title: Deepfake fraud is handled as ordinary cheating, with no AI-specific evidence protocol
gaps.basis: Scam cases are booked under general cheating and IT Act personation provisions. Police could not confirm whether a deepfake was used (IN-INC-03). No forensic standard for detecting synthetic media in evidence was found.

gaps.title: Personality rights rely on case-by-case injunctions
gaps.basis: Voice and likeness cloning relief comes from court orders for well-known individuals. No statutory right reaches ordinary people targeted by deepfakes.

gaps.title: Public-sector algorithms lack disclosure and contestability
gaps.basis: RTI requests for Samagra Vedika source code were refused on the vendor’s rights. NITI Aayog principles flag exclusion risk, but no binding audit or explanation duty applies to state eligibility systems.

gaps.title: No verification rule for AI-assisted legal citations
gaps.basis: Two incidents of non-existent precedents reached adjudication. No court-wide practice direction on AI use was found in this research.

gaps.title: SGI labelling rules exclude text, and chatbot output liability is unsettled
gaps.basis: The 2026 rules cover audio-visual synthetic content only. Whether an AI developer is an intermediary for its chatbot’s answers remains unclear (IN-INC-05).

survey.intro: This survey asks practitioners who work on AI in India to rate which AI risks matter most here. It adapts the structure of the MIT AI Risk Initiative expert survey (severity, likelihood, vulnerability, responsibility) to Indian conditions. It takes about 6 minutes.
